Part One · The theater of prevention

The Deterrent

Nature invented the art of scaring off trouble before it starts. The automotive industry spent a century reinventing it, loudly, and getting it almost entirely wrong.

By Oliver Bacon · 13 minute read

Deterrents have been around roughly since there has been anything worth taking. The idea — make the harm go away before it happens, rather than surviving it afterwards — is one of evolution's better ideas, and it long predates anything with a steering wheel.

Consider three animals that solved the same problem three completely different ways. The porcupine went armored: up to thirty thousand quills, barbed at the tip, designed to detach on contact and work their way inward. The skunk went chemical: a spray of sulfur compounds accurate to several meters that does not injure anything but makes the encounter so comprehensively unpleasant that nothing repeats it. And the king snake — harmless, entirely non-venomous — simply put on the colors of the coral snake and let its neighbor's reputation do the work.

Three strategies: hurt them, disgust them, or bluff them. None is perfect. Nothing is, except death and taxes.

Worth noting on the porcupine, because almost everyone has this wrong: it cannot throw its quills. It has never been able to throw its quills. The entire fearsome reputation rests on a defense that only functions if something is already touching it — and it works anyway, because the reputation arrived first. Hold that thought. It is going to come back.

Fig. 1Three strategies, and what the car industry made of them

Injure

Physical cost

The porcupine. Raise the price of contact so high that nothing is willing to pay it. Requires no communication and no bluff — only follow-through.

Automotive equivalent
Locks, steering bars, kill switches
Slows the determined thief. Does not stop one.

Repel

Sensory cost

The skunk. Do no lasting damage at all; simply make the experience intolerable and unforgettable. Works on memory rather than injury.

Automotive equivalent
The audible alarm
Failed — because unlike a skunk, it went off constantly.

Bluff

Borrowed reputation

The king snake. Carry no weapon whatsoever; wear the warning colors of something that does. Costs nothing and works entirely on what the observer already believes.

Automotive equivalent
The blinking red LED on the dash
Still works. Costs about a dollar.

The pattern to watch: the two strategies that depend on the thief believing something have aged far better than the one that depends on making a noise.

One

The hardest thing you own to protect

A car is a strange kind of possession. It is among the most expensive things most people will ever buy. It has to be maintained, insured, serviced and looked after. And unlike almost anything else of comparable value, it is engineered from the outset to sit outdoors and weather whatever the sky does to it — which is exactly why we stopped thinking of leaving it out as a risk at all. And then — for most of us, most of the time — it sits unattended, in the dark, on a public street.

Almost nothing else we own gets treated this way. Spend comparable money on anything else and it goes somewhere with a door and a lock. The car gets a curb and good wishes. Rain it can handle. Hail, road salt, ten Julys in a parking lot — all designed for. What it was never designed to survive is the other thing it is left exposed to, which is people.

And because cars are desirable, a certain number of people conclude that they too are entitled to enjoy the car, or at the very least whatever has been left on the passenger seat. If you are reading this there is a reasonable chance you have been on the wrong end of it. I have, twice — once for the whole car, once for the contents, and neither was the character-building experience people promise.

Although I will admit to one genuinely surreal detail. On the break-in, whoever it was left behind a small pile of somebody else's belongings in my car. Not a trade I agreed to. Not a trade I'd have accepted. But there is something almost courteous about a burglar who treats the whole thing as an exchange.

659,880Vehicles stolen in the US, 2025
−23%Change from 2024, itself down 17%
1 in ~440Annual odds per registered vehicle
48 secInterval between thefts, nationally

Those odds deserve one clarification, because the number moves depending on what you divide by, and people are routinely careless about it. Roughly 660,000 thefts against something like 290 million registered vehicles is about one in 440 — per vehicle. Measured against the population instead, it is closer to one in 500 people per year. Both are true. They are not the same statistic, and figures quoted from a few years ago will run considerably higher than either, because the ground has shifted enormously since 2023.

Theft from a vehicle — smashed window, rifled glovebox, gone in ninety seconds — runs several times more common than theft of the vehicle itself. And the uncomfortable finding that surfaces repeatedly in police prevention data is that a very large share of it involves no forced entry at all. Unlocked doors and visible valuables do most of the work. Roughly a third happens where the owner lives: driveways, apartment lots, the spot directly outside the front door.

The most effective anti-theft device ever devised is remembering to take the bag off the seat.Unglamorous, free, and statistically dominant

So what can be done? Honestly, less than anyone selling security hardware would like you to believe. The moment you park something valuable outdoors you have entered a negotiation with everyone who walks past it. But deterrents are the best instrument available, and they have come a very long way — mostly by learning, slowly and expensively, which of the three animal strategies actually transfers to a parked car.

Two

A hundred and thirty years of trying

The problem is as old as the product. The first recorded car theft is generally dated to Paris in 1896, when a mechanic made off with Baron de Zuylen's Peugeot — an unusually pointed target, given that the Baron had co-founded the Automobile Club of France. Car, and thief, were recovered.

What followed was a century of invention that reads, in hindsight, like a list of increasingly sophisticated ways to be ignored.

Fig. 2The anti-theft device, 1896–2026

Read the top row against the bottom. Every device above the line announces itself to the thief. Every device below it works silently, and those are the ones that changed the numbers.

The earliest answers were disarmingly literal. Around the turn of the century one solution was simply to make the steering wheel removable, so the driver could carry it away and leave a spindle behind. It is easy to laugh, but the logic is impeccable, and it is the exact same logic the entire industry would rediscover ninety years later with the immobilizer: take one necessary component away with you and the vehicle is furniture.

Alarms arrived next. The origin story most often repeated dates to 1913 and an unnamed prisoner in Denver, credited with a device that rang a bell when somebody turned the starting crank. Within a few years the trade press was reporting wireless variations on the idea. Then in 1918, two inventors named St. George Evans and Edward Birkenbeuel patented something considerably more devious: a grid of switches that had to be set to a particular combination before the car would start. Get it wrong and the current was diverted to the horn, which then sounded until the battery gave out.

Which is worth sitting with, because that 1918 patent is not really an alarm. It is an immobilizer with a temper — a device that both prevents the theft and announces it. The industry then spent the better part of eighty years separating those two functions and backing the wrong one.

The first genuinely mass-market aftermarket alarm arrived in 1954: a unit that lived in the glovebox with wires run to the doors, hood and trunk, and a master switch mounted somewhere on the car's exterior. Open anything without disarming it first and the horn went off. Factory-fitted systems followed in the early 1970s, with Chrysler among the first to offer them across full-size models, and General Motors fitting alarms to the Corvette. By the mid-seventies the aftermarket had discovered the remote control, and the modern car alarm — armed from a distance, chirping to confirm it — had essentially arrived.

Three

The tragedy of the car alarm

Here is where the skunk analogy breaks down, and the reason is arithmetic rather than engineering.

A skunk's defense works because it is rare, unambiguous, and never deployed by accident. A car alarm is none of those things. Fitted to a few thousand cars in a city, a siren is a genuine emergency signal and heads turn. Fitted to a few million, set to a sensitivity that will trigger on a passing bus, a thunderclap, a heavy bassline or a cat, it becomes weather. And people do not investigate weather.

This is not a retrospective judgment invented by columnists. By 1994 the New York City Police Department was publicly making a far sharper argument — not merely that alarms had stopped working, but that they may have been making vehicle crime more frequent. And there is a documented account from New York two years earlier of a thief who worked out the logical conclusion before anyone else: he deliberately rocked a car until its own alarm went off, and then broke the window, because the siren covered the sound of the glass.

The deterrent had become the cover.New York, 1992

That is the whole failure in one image. A device sold as protection, repurposed as camouflage, by the very people it was sold to repel.

Fig. 3Why every audible deterrent eventually eats itself

Conceptual, not measured — the shape of the problem rather than a data series. The audible alarm is unusual among security devices in that its effectiveness depends on how few other people have one. Adoption is self-defeating. Locks, immobilizers and cameras have no such property.

The consequence shows up in what manufacturers quietly stopped doing. Many carmakers moved away from fitting simple noise-makers as the primary defense, and shifted to silent immobilizers instead — a system that never tells the thief anything, and never tells the neighbors anything either. The alarm survives on modern cars mostly as a secondary flourish. The actual work moved elsewhere, which is the subject of the second half of this piece.

Popular culture got there well before the criminologists. The 1988 comedy Twins contains a sequence in which Danny DeVito's character is sitting in a Cadillac he has no business sitting in, the alarm goes off precisely as designed, and Arnold Schwarzenegger's character resolves the matter by strolling around to the back and picking the car up. The siren keeps going. Nobody comes. It is a very good joke about brute force beating electronics, and a better one about how completely everybody had stopped caring. Schwarzenegger has since admitted the lift itself was movie magic — too many takes, and a genuinely stupid risk. The indifference was documentary.

Four

The Club, and the return of the visible

By the 1990s the public had worked out what the data would later confirm: an alarm on its own was not keeping anyone's car. So security went backwards, deliberately, to something a thief could see through the window from three meters away.

A wave of third-party devices arrived built on a single premise: let them get in, let them even start it, but make it impossible to actually drive away without doing obvious damage or spending obvious time. The best-selling of them by a distance was the Club — a long steel bar that clamped across the steering wheel with a hooked jaw at each end. The logic was elegant. You cannot turn a wheel more than a few degrees when a heavy bar bolted to it fouls the windshield and the door card on every rotation.

What the design did not adequately account for is that the bar was never the weak point. You would need something close to four silverback gorillas to defeat the Club itself. You need considerably less to defeat the thing it is attached to. A hacksaw through the steering wheel rim — a hoop of thin steel wrapped in foam and plastic — and the whole assembly slides off in about a minute, entirely intact, still locked, and now completely irrelevant.

Its relatives had the same blind spot. There was a variant that anchored the steering wheel to the brake pedal, on the theory that a car you cannot stop is a car you cannot steal. It could still accelerate. And it could still be freed the same way, by cutting the wheel and unhooking the pedal end.

Fig. 4Where the Club actually fails

The lock was never the weak point. Every steering-wheel device of this generation secured itself to a component thinner and softer than the device itself — which is a design problem, not a manufacturing one.

And yet. Sales were enormous, and the reason has nothing to do with any of the above. Almost nobody stood in a parking lot sawing through a steering wheel, because almost nobody needed to. They looked in the window, saw two feet of bright yellow steel, and went to the next car, which did not have any.

Which makes the Club not a lock at all. It is the king snake. It is warning coloration — and the fact that it can be defeated in sixty seconds matters far less than the fact that the car beside it can be defeated in ten.

This is the uncomfortable heart of visible deterrence. It does not reduce theft. It relocates it. Every driver who bought a Club in 1993 bought a small, real, measurable improvement in their own odds, purchased directly from their neighbor. Nothing was prevented. Something was moved.

A deterrent that only works because the car next to you doesn't have one is not a solution. It is a queue.The limit of visible security

Which raises the obvious question. If a century of locks, sirens, bars and bluffs mostly shuffled theft around rather than stopping it — then something else must explain what happened next. Because starting in the early 1990s, American car theft did not move. It collapsed. It fell by eighty percent and it stayed down for thirty years.

It was not the alarm. It was not the Club. It was a component that costs a few dollars, has no moving parts, makes no sound whatsoever, and that almost nobody who owns one could point to.
